She told a story of how she had been burned out of her house in a town just north of Prijedor called Bosanski Novi and described a very frightening 90-kilometre round robin hike sometimes with fellow deportees. She said she saw them killing people by the road. Eventually she said she and her friend had been taken in by some Serbs to make coffee for them for a while before being allowed to cross the river Una into Bosanska Krupa and then to Bihac. I wrote down and have written that she made coffee for the Serbs. I know now what that meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The town itself, was it under attack during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, under fairly heavy attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was the town being shelled during that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was, especially towards nightfall, and the United Nations military observers were pointing out that it was being shelled not only from the Bosnian Serb side but also fairly intensively from the Bosnian Croat side as well -- sorry, from the -- forgive me, the Croatian Serbian side, that is to say, the Croatian Krajina, from the west as well as from the east and south, that is to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you personally have an opportunity to observe the formations of the Croatian Serb military forces on the other side of the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The United Nations military observer who was from the Royal Air Force of my country, actually, a man called Millington, he was very, very angry indeed about this, angry at his own employer as well, and he advised us to go to a Bosnian army encampment on a high plain above Cazin where there's a turkey farm and from which he said you could see quite clearly from whence the fire was coming into Bihac from the Croatian Serbian side, in addition to from the Bosnian Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you, in fact, see those positions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you could see the guns firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you note was happening at that turkey farm with regard to the Bosnian military forces at that point?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: The Bosnian so-called army at that point was quartered on this turkey farm and I didn't spend a great deal of time there, but the -- the single memory I have of the place was that bullets were being issued and signed for singly, one round at a time, which gave some kind of indication of the weaponry that they had at their disposal. The men went to the front-line from the farm and from the centre of town on the bus, on civilian buses, and they were unarmed when they went up there and I remember we said to them, "Well, where are your weapons?" They said, "Oh, they're on the front-line already. The shift that comes off gives us the guns and we take over from them that way." So there were more men than weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Do you recall any particular attacks during the time that you were in Bihac?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Two. One -- if there was any debate from whence the firing was coming, we were driving back into the town on the western side and were shot at from Croatia, in effect, but the most memorable attacks were around and on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And what occurred at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: The hospital was working as best it could to treat people. Like many hospitals that I visited in Bosnia, it was -- they were having to work often without anaesthetic, and there was one -- a shell was levelled at the hospital on one occasion while I was there, but the occasion I'll -- I remember most vividly was the admission into the hospital of a seven year old girl who had been hit in the head by a sniper's bullet, and I was told this was while she was running across her back garden with her mother, their house having been hit by a mortar, and this girl was bandaged up and they asked us to come over and have a look, and she was almost unconscious, her eyes were shut, and I just put my hand under her shoulder, I was -- I wasn't thinking professionally at the time, and there was this horrible shudder and that was, it turned out, the moment of her death. That's the most memorable attack on Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During -- at the same time as the attacks on Bihac were being conducted both from within Bosnia and from Croatia by the Croatian Serbian forces, did you become aware that there were also attacks in the south of Bosnia by Yugoslav Army forces?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry, in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Did you become aware that at the same time that -- during the same period that you were in Bihac, there were attacks by the Yugoslav Army in the south of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, down in southeast -- Montenegrin -- the Montenegrin divisions where colleagues had been reporting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If you could briefly review that exhibit, Mr. Vulliamy? I believe we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With respect to this exhibit, we have an objection. Clearly in accordance with the Court's ruling confining at least some of the different conflicts, different flare-ups and wars that occurred in Bosnia, this particular one, Prevlaka, or Dubrovnik area, and if you look on your respective maps, I think Exhibit 43, the map, you will see that Dubrovnik is clearly designated in the Croatian side all the way in the centre of your map, significantly -- right by the sea there, if not extensively-- and Prevlaka is in that area, removed from the Prijedor area which we're concerned with here, but definitely it's outside the scope of your instruction as well, so we object on those grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might? The report which of course is an article by the Belgrade press agency TANJUG, which was the state news agency in the former Yugoslavia, is reporting the statement by the president of the Serb Autonomous Region of Herzegovina, which, as you heard in earlier testimony, is within Bosnia and Herzegovina, was one of the Serb Autonomous Regions declared by the Bosnian Serbs. They are discussing here members of the Yugoslav Army Podgorica corps, which is the capital of Montenegro, being deployed east of Dubrovnik -- it's actually in Bosnia-Herzegovina territory, and the town specifically mentioned is Trebinje, which you will note on that map is, in fact, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this is within 1992, it is within Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it does relate to international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, from Bihac, where was the next area in 1992 that you went to cover?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, for a number of weeks, I was preoccupied with the emergent conflict between the Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, and then, fairly suddenly, our attention was drawn back to Travnik by the fall of the town of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And where, in relation to Travnik, is the town of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Jajce is to the northwest of Travnik and was under heavy siege. It's a mixed Muslim and Croat town -- was -- and was under Serb siege. We had tried to -- or I with colleagues had tried to get to Jajce a number of times through a very narrow sort of umbilical corridor which serviced the town. By night ammunition and supplies and food would be taken up. We tried to go up that corridor a number of times but were prevented from doing so by very heavy fire across it. So I never actually got to Jajce, but it fell during the very last days of October and the first days in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: At some point was the evacuation of Jajce ordered?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I think at a certain point the Croatian HVO army first realised that the town was under such heavy fire it was now indefensible and pulled off the lines, the Bosnian army followed, and they ordered the people to leave, such was the intensity of the bombardment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And did you witness, in fact, the evacuation of Jajce within that corridor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Late one evening, we went up as far as a village called Turbe on the frontlines, and the first few people started straggling in from Jajce with stories of their town ablaze. It was the next day, Saturday, I think November the 1st, something like that, it was the Saturday that we went out to a midpoint called Karaule, between Turbe and Jajce, and beheld this scene of some 40.000, according to the UNHCR, people coming down the lanes with carts, horses, sheep, farm animals, a defeated army, beating this pathetic retreat. They were under fire as they did so, and I know that because in a fairly quiet moment between Karaule and Turbe, there was a sudden shot and a man wounded in the arm while he was riding on the back of a horse-drawn cart.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The people that you witnessed being evacuated from Jajce, what type of people were coming down that road? Were they all military forces or related to the military?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, no. The military were a small minority. They were as anxious to hitch a ride on the carts, the horse-drawn carts, as anybody else, but for the most part, this was -- these were rural people, civilians, families, children, old people, anybody. It was the population of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you speak to the people that were in this column or convoy coming down this road?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: We spoke to them mostly -- yes, a few on the convoy, but mostly when they encamped in the streets of Travnik and any open space they could find. I remember thinking and writing at the time this looked like something out of Tolstoy, these broilers, horses, sheep wandering everywhere, people were bringing their farms literally with them. This was an incredible sight, Travnik, as I've said, already very full, and we talked to them, yes, about the intensifying bombardment of their town and the way in which they had, towards the end, been mostly living in cellars and had to come out to get food when the two defending armies had boarded up the corridor for them to collect and going down into the cellars to eat it again, they talked about attacks on their fleeing convoy, and we spent the rest of the day having conversations along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you determine the ethnic groups of the people to whom you spoke?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. And they were divided about 50-50 Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You indicated that they described to you the intensifying shelling of the town. Did they describe to you how the siege of the town had been conducted?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was mostly artillery and mortar fire, and the -- it was the military people rather than the civilians who told us that they had heard word that the time had really come for them to surrender because reinforcements had been brought, they had been told, from Belgrade, JNA reinforcements, to finish off the job. The Serbs were anxious, I think, to -- Jajce was something of a promontory jutting into their territory, and they were anxious to clear it out of the way and clean up their frontline so as to better lay siege to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they -- you referred to statements that the -- people as they were evacuating the town had been shelled.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was quite a lot of discussion about how, as the convoys were being formed, one man talked about having to scramble up a mud bank because it was a wet weekend and that they were open-fired upon when they tried to scramble up this mud bank to form the convoy to get out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In the very few days after these events which you just described, did the ICRC issue a press release on the situation in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they did. I think -- I remember reporting it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: May I have that marked as the next exhibit, Exhibit 55, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 54, that will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm sorry, 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, do you recognise --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: -- that press release?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Yes, I do. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Is that the press release issued by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: And it's dated ... The date of the press release?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: The 4th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, the final area in Bosnia with respect to events in 1992 I'd like to cover with you deals with the area -- the areas of Sarajevo and Visegrad. Can you please describe your experiences in Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Like everybody covering this war, I was in and out of Sarajevo, although mostly after the dates that we're going to talk about. But during 1992, I was able to visit both sides of the siege. I was able to -- I got quite a tour of the Serb siege lines on the day that we were in Pale, while we were waiting to go down to Kula. We were taken on a tour by two soldiers, and so we were able to tour with them and look down on the town from the hills from which the siege was being laid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: From the viewpoint of those gun positions, could you see the various sections of the city below?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Very easily. Sarajevo is in a bowl, surrounded by mountains, high ground and, yes, it's laid out like a map, a city plan beneath you. You can see it very easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you pick out particular landmarks within the city from those positions?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, indeed. You can see the various churches, the Holiday Inn, the library, which by then had been destroyed, and various landmarks, well-known, yes. With binoculars, of course, even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Could you see clearly apartment buildings and homes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. With binoculars you could almost see cars and people, if they were powerful enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you, while you were up at those Serbian gun positions, have conversations with the people who were escorting you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did. There was a gesture of bravado by one of the soldiers, he made to spray the whole city with his -- he didn't actually shoot, he just pretended to spray the whole city with his gun and said the only good Muslim is a dead Muslim and various jokes about how many wives they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, when did you actually begin to study the area of Visegrad and report on what occurred there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the war, it was the only time I was able to get into Visegrad to research what had happened in that area. It was a roundabout route, some men had been taken from Srebrenica to Dublin and I was invited to talk to them. One clearly seemed much to young to be in the army. I said; "What were you doing in 1992? How old were you?" He said he was 13. I asked him what did he do then as he was then in the pocket of Zepa. He said my job was to get the bodies out of the river. And I said which bodies? He said the bodies that were being thrown off the bridge in Visegrad. And I was amazed at what he was telling me and how many bodies were involved and the condition they were in. Some of them, he said, decapitated and many of them children, and because the bridge in Visegrad is so famous, I made it my business to try and investigate what had been going on there in what would have been the spring to summer months of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Your usual objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Actually, I'm a little more disturbed, Your Honour, and quite frankly I want the Court to direct its attention, if you have the Tadic Exhibit 1423 and that page, specifically Mr. Vulliamy states it was in the Visegrad area and he describes the same scenes here he's telling us or sharing with us here, but those were made -- I know he's trying to reference what occurred several years ago, but he was there during this visit and during this conversation in 1996, and he plainly states that in Tadic, and just so that we're clear, and I'm only asking this Court to perhaps adopt this, that if he's discussing something that he saw, that he's more explicit with the dates that he claims he's discussing it, because clearly in Tadic, there's a grave inconsistency, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can cross-examine about that in due course, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Keegan, I think what we should be clear, is the witness describing something he saw himself or merely something that he had reported to him rather later, which seems to be the understanding which I have of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The testimony describes events which occurred in '92. The witness, in his testimony, is talking about reports given to him in '96, and then he'll talk about travelling to Visegrad and speaking with Bosnian Serbs on the other side about 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We shan't admit this evidence. We're really getting too far away from the subject matter, and it being a report by somebody about events which happened in Visegrad, we're not inclined to admit it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour? I would at least respectfully request a proffer on where the evidence will go because I believe that, in fact, if the witness confirmed with Bosnian Serbs that hundreds of bodies were -- of Muslims were killed and thrown into the river during the same period in 1992 as we're talking about in Prijedor to the point where it was plugging up the culverts of the hydro electric dam, then that does describe events that would be in consideration on the question of the widespread nature of the attack and the purpose of the attacks going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The evidence we've been hearing from the witness has been about events in 1992 in Bosnia which he witnessed or was very close to or were reported to him at the same time. Now what you're trying to admit is the evidence of somebody who was 13 at the time -- that may not matter much -- but a report given four years later referring to events in 1992 in Visegrad, the other side of Bosnia. Now, we have said throughout that we will admit hearsay and we have done, and we allow great latitude in the evidence which is admitted, but we are ruling that this particular piece of evidence is too remote and too much hearsay and too far from Prijedor to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I note that it's just about 3.30. The remainder of the testimony then would be the interviews in 1996 with the accused and with Milomir Stakic. It might be better to begin that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would be appropriate. How long do you think you will be?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thirty minutes maybe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, in 1996, did you return to Prijedor to conduct some interviews?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: During the time you were there, did you interview both Milomir Stakic and the accused?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Where is it that you found Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I met him -- we met him, I was travelling with a colleague, at the health centre in Prijedor, of which I believe he was the director, a day care health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there anyone else present with him in the office for the interview?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. With Dr. Stakic there was a man called Mr. Kondic who was variously introduced with a number of titles and with me was a colleague from the New York Times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, during the course of this interview, did you ask him generally about what had happened in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and he had argued that the Serbs were defending themselves, but that most of the conversation, what I wanted to talk to him, out of curiosity, really, was about Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What did he say about Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, initially he said that there was no one collected into Omarska, that -- we asked him about the television pictures, and he said that they were pictures of Serbian prisoners in Muslim gaols and that the story was fabricated. He said, "If you're a journalist, you have to be on the spot to know what's going on," and I remember biting my tongue at that point because I had not declared myself as having been there personally. But he said that Omarska -- "No one was collected into that place," he said. And Mr. Kondic interrupted and said, "Omarska was a mine, nothing else," is as accurate as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they later change their version of what had occurred in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Almost immediately there was this curious negation of what he had just said. Dr. Stakic said that, "In Omarska, there were only those Muslims who were under interrogation for," and I paraphrase here but I can produce the exact words, if asked, "They were under interrogation for possession of arms or military activity, and that once a proper prisoner of war camp had been established, only those arrested with illegal weapons were kept in that place."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him whether there had been any killing at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't recall asking Mr. Stakic that. I might have done. But we moved on from Omarska to the general theme of camps and the Serbian experience of camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he make any reference to Jasenovac during your interview?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. All conversations about Omarska refer back to Jasenovac, and he said that it was wrong to make any comparison between the two, that Omarska was not a concentration camp, he said, and he said that the Serbs fight when their freedom is threatened, and Mr. Kondic added at this point, "Unfortunately, we, the Serbs, have learned to defend our freedom in concentration camps," which was a reference to Jasenovac. So there was this invocation of the camp experience throughout the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did they make reference to the conditions that the prisoners had in Omarska in the context of this conversation regarding Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stakic said, "You can't compare them." He said that in Omarska, the prisoners, they had food. He said the prisoners in Omarska had doctors; they didn't work. And then he said -- and I remember this well -- he said Omarska was not a hotel, and he smiled a rather unpleasant smile and said, "But it was not a concentration camp."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he make a reference to when or if the Serbs will go to extremes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, he said, "The Serbs will go to extremes when their freedom or if their freedom is threatened."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Was there a discussion about the relationship of the Serbian people in Yugoslavia during this conflict?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Like Mr. Kovacevic back in Prijedor four years before, he said that the Serbs -- and he specified the Serbs in this area -- are arriving at a great moment in their history, and he said that, quote: "When the Serbs have been at war for four years, there are no Krajina Serbs, Bosnian Serbs, or Serbian Serbs, there are just Serbs."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, why is it that you chose to reinterview the accused, Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was curious to know what kind of people had been introduced to me as being responsible for Omarska, I was curious to know what kind of people -- on whose authority we had gone to the camps. I then thought, and was corrected, actually, because he said, in 1992, that he had been born in Jasenovac. I found this an intriguing situation. Omarska and its inmates had, in a way, followed me throughout the war, I kept bumping into them in various places within the war and beyond it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: The question was why, of the other people in the Prijedor area that you met, why did you specifically choose to interview, re-interview, Kovacevic? What was it about him or your experiences with him that led you to re-interview him?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was a result of the meeting in the civic centre in Prijedor. We had gone through this recap only briefly, we had gone through this -- Colonel Arsic had wanted us to go to Manjaca. We said no. He said, "Oh, well, if you want to go to Omarska, talk to these people," and he gestured, Mr. Kovacevic and next to him Mr. Stakic. Mr. Drljaca I also tried to interview on that trip but he was not available. I wanted to see them all, but Kovacevic in particular because he had opened the meeting, he had chaired the meeting, he had been the man who, when the television journalists went back to Omarska after I had left Serbia, had been put up to defend the place on television, he was well-known; and indeed, at the end of Mr. Stakic's presentation, when he was saying, "Go to Manjaca" and we said "No," he shrugged and said, "Well, if you want to go to Omarska, talk to this man."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Who was he referring to when he said that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Kovacevic, who was sitting next to him. And so I wanted to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Now, during your earlier evidence regarding the meeting in 1992, you referred to a map which the accused got out and discussed. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the map was by the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Can you please describe what that map was and what was the general statement made by the accused with respect to that map?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the map was published or -- I mean the original dated from the early 1940s, 1941, and was a map of Serbia as envisaged at that time wherever the Serbs lived -- I don't recall whether it said Greater Serbia or not, but that's the term used to describe the area covered. It comprised most of -- a lot of Croatia; as I recall, all, if not most, of Bosnia-Herzegovina and what is now Serbia and Montenegro; and we were shown this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: How did the accused refer to the map at that time? What was the point of him showing it to the group of reporters?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I think it is, "This is where the Serbs are. This is Serbia. This is the idea."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he relate it to why the conflict was being conducted at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not specifically, but I understood it to mean "This is what we're fighting for."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: In this interview in 1996, did you discuss with him or did you raise the issue of the causes of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was a long conversation, and he was very candid and interesting on the subject. He said he thought it was a civil war, basically a religious war, but he said there were economic factors - which was interesting to hear him say that because it was an interesting dimension - but he was most interesting on the sort of psychiatric dimension, and he said at one point, "It's all very well if your view is from New York, but here on the ground, when everything is burning and breaking apart in people's heads, this was something for the psychiatrists." And he was very lucid on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did he describe what the point of the conflict was from his perspective, what his point in the conflict was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, very, very candidly. He said that "I wanted to make this Serb land." One of us asked him, "What do you mean? Without Muslims?" And he said, "Without Muslims, yes. We cannot live together."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him questions relating specifically to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: What was his comment about the purpose of Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: He said that Omarska was intended as a collection centre but, he said, "It turned into something else because of this loss of control." I think we asked him something like, "What loss of control?" And he said, "I cannot explain this loss of control," and I think I've already said it's "when everything's breaking apart in people's heads." He said, "I would call it collective madness."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him about how many people had been killed in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This was during a section of the conversation again about Jasenovac, which we discussed at length because of him having said earlier he had been born there. He said that in Omarska, only 100 people -- well, at first he said, "Whether it was ten or 100, it doesn't matter." And then we said, "Were only 100 people killed in Omarska?" And he said, "I said 'killed,' not died.'" And we said, "How many died?" And he said, "I don't know. You'll have to ask the doctors." And then said, "Oh, I don't know how many people were killed in Omarska," and I quote, "It's like a hurricane around" -- sorry. He said something about, and I quote, "The hurricane blowing to and fro around here."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: You mentioned Jasenovac. Was there, in fact, conversations comparing Omarska and Jasenovac?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, at length. He recalled his childhood in Jasenovac. He hadn't actually been born there, he said, in the event, he had gone there with his aunt and gave a very credible and vivid description of his mother being led away and he went to Jasenovac where his aunt saved him. The comparison or contrast, to be fair, he made was that he said that in Omarska, maybe people were killed if somebody got drunk and got mad, but -- and at this point he said, "But if it was ten or a hundred, it doesn't matter." "But Josenovac was a killing factory," he said, "Omarska was not a killing factory."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him what the link was between what had occurred between the Ustasha and the Serbs in Jasenovac and the Serbs and the Muslims in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and on this again he was very lucid. He said that there was a direct connection between Jasenovac and Omarska, but, he said, it is a thin one. He said the fact that there were Muslim soldiers in the Greater Croatia during the war had had an effect on what happened to the Muslims in this area. He said -- he had a rather -- we said to him back, "But hold on. Jasenovac was run by Croats. What has that got to do with the Muslims?" And Mr. Kovacevic came up with quite a bon mots. He said, "If you're bitten by a snake, you can still be afraid of lizards, but a snake is still a snake and a lizard is still a lizard," to which my colleague from The New York Times said, "Oh, you mean the Muslims are the lizards, but you're still scared of them?" And he said "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him questions about the responsibility for what had occurred, who had the responsibility for what had occurred?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in the historic sense, he went back to the war. He said that "There were Muslims in the Ustasha, and if they committed war crimes against us, then now it is the same the other way around." And he had the insight to say that "Who knows? In 50 years' time, it could happen the other way around again." And then I remember we asked him, "This collective madness, Doctor, were you part of it?" And he said, "If I was to be acquitted of being a part of this collective madness, that would not be right, but I would want to ask myself what my part in it was." And then he said, "If Dusko Tadic killed people and I did not, then that is not the same thing." And he added, "If things go well in this hospital, if everything is fine in this hospital, then I am to be commended, but if things go wrong in this hospital, then I'm guilty." He went on to talk about why he left political life and was clearly -- he was most articulate on that. He said he had left politics because he saw too many "evil things." Then I think we said, "Well, what things?" He said, "That is my personal secret. If you have to do things by killing people, that is my personal secret." I think it was my colleague from The New York Times who said, "Do you ever have nightmares about your personal secrets, sir?" And he said, quote: "My hair is white. I do not sleep too well."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you ask him about comparisons between the situation in the Balkans and talking about the perspective of people in Europe?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he made some joke about the Una being a border. He said "This isn't Europe, this is the Balkans." At one point he said, "We don't have evolution here, we have revolution," and became chatty about it. He said, "I want to get out." He said, "I'm like an animal in a cage. I want to go to Paris or Berlin to work and practice my profession."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Did you bring the interview down onto a more personal level? Did you discuss his personal experiences or that of his family with the Muslims who formerly lived in the area?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, quite apart from Jasenovac. And, yes, he talked about his father and how he had been a farmer and had dealt with the Muslims and had sold cattle to the Muslims, and how he had always -- his father always called them Turks, and then conceded, he said, "Well, actually, they aren't really Turks at all. They come from here."

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: We have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it Valumay (phonetic) or Vulliamy?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's whatever you like, sir. It's Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Vulliamy? Thank you. Mr. Vulliamy, you spoke a little bit about the notes that you kept and records. To whom, if anyone, did you give those notes regarding the various interviews and regarding the various times that you spent in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: To whom did I give them?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If anyone.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, when I was called to appear here, I gave them to the court -- well, I was asked for them, but I didn't -- I haven't handed them around to anybody else, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can appreciate that. When was the first time that you handed your personal notes that were taken involving the Yugoslavia - Bosnia and Herzegovina civil war?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I would have to consult and come back if you want an exact date, but it would be when I was first called to testify in 1996 for the Prosecution of Dusko Tadic in this court. It would have been sometime during the spring, I imagine, of that year, if not slightly prior.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that '96?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I thought. Now, did you give them the originals or copies of those notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of my shorthand?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the books, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you recreate from your shorthand notes a typewritten form of those notes?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: In some cases, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now -- and I asked a compound question and you answered it properly, and it was my mistake. I asked if you gave them the original or a copy, and I think you answered in the affirmative, and again, it's my mistake. Did you give the Prosecutors your original notes involving what you had seen and experienced in Bosnia-Herzegovina during the civil war in 1992 through whatever period it was?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you're a journalist by profession; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: From where did you obtain your journalism degree?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: In England, we don't really have journalism degrees like you do in America. You have what's called an indenture and you go on a training; and in my case, this was a company owned by the Mirror Group who had a series of "stable newspapers," as they're called, in the West of England, in Devonshire.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The name of the group was Mirror Group?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mirror Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did you obtain that -- or the completion of that study or course?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I apologise for going in your history a little bit --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- because I actually didn't get all the notes --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- and I apologise to the Court as well. You mentioned the study of philosophy. Do you recall that early on in your testimony? What year did you obtain your philosophical degree -- or philosophy degree?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I got my degree from Oxford in 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned political science. What year did you obtain or confer that degree?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: They're coupled together. It's a degree at Oxford called PPE, which stands for Politics, Philosophy, and Economics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And then you mentioned Florence, that you studied in Italy. Did you obtain a degree from a university in Florence?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a diploma from Florence which I started in '73 but I didn't go back to collect it until '76.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What degree was that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's not a degree, it's called a diploma in Renaissance Studies. It would be wrong to call it a degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise. What diploma was that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's called Renaissance Studies. It's a fairly minor thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: During your studies of political science at Oxford, did you study at all Eastern Europe?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. The Soviet Union in great detail, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you study at all Yugoslavia or what has now been referred to as the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was part of the Eastern Bloc bit of the course. "The Political Institutions of the USSR," it was called, but we had to learn all about non-alignment and Tito and the Warsaw Pact and so on, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many courses would that have been that you studied, just out of curiosity, about Eastern Europe and particularly Yugoslavia? That's what interests us, I believe.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: "The Political Institutions of the USSR," which was the title of the course into which Yugoslavia came, would have been one part of eight papers, one of eight papers that you took over a period of two years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you shared with us some of your professional --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Three years, sorry. You had a thing called prelims for the first year and then you did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You shared with us a little bit about your professional experience, and I want to just expand upon that a little bit. Other than a journalist, do you have any other professional experience?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not really. I left university, Oxford University, in the summer of '76; I went to Italy, to Florence, until the spring of '77; I came back and I started with the Mirror Group in the summer of 1977. I went to Granada Television in 1978, and since then -- unless you count television as a different profession, it's all I've done.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can take just from your testimony that you haven't been educated at all -- and I say that respectfully just because you haven't mentioned it -- in any medical disciplines at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Medical disciplines, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can I take, from your professional background and history, that you've never been an elected official of any either municipality or any community or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about an appointed position? Have you ever been in an appointed position?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Clearly none important. I was the Secretary of the Hartford College Oxford Arts Society. I think that's the only office I've ever held or ever want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is that a political --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: About as apolitical as you can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's what I thought. I'm just concerned with appointments in a political nature, if any?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with respect again to your background both professional and personal, any military experience?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I have military in the family, but not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you had never served either voluntarily or involuntarily in any military unit at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I have a general and a colonel in the extended family, but I have no military experience, although I have had experience of wars.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the experience on wars is actually a topic that I want to discuss with you. I know, just from your discussions here today, you talked about the civil war in Yugoslavia and Bosnia, and you talked about Northern Ireland, I think, a little bit, here and in the Tadic trial. Did you cover the war at all in South Africa?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you cover the war at all in the Middle East?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What period of time did you?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: 1993, I was in Israel, the West Bank, and very briefly in southern Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In 1993, when you were in Israel, for what period of time were you there?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry. This is -- 1983. Forgive me. 1983, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought you said '93 --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: The year after the Lebanon war, right? Sorry about that. 1983. It was for about a month or so, month or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about any civil wars or the break-up of the old Soviet Union, the former Soviet Union?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was in Romania in the Christmas period of 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was there during Caucescu --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: That was the downfall of Caucescu and the, as was thought at the time, revolution against the Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May we have a moment, Your Honour? Excuse me. Just so the court knows, I've been instructed to slow down the speech, and I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in 1983, did you, during the Israeli and south Lebanon and your experiences in 1983, did you report on any detention centres or camps occurring at that time at all?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not at such.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Any time in your experience, other than the experience that you've had currently through 1992, currently, have you reported on such detention centres or camps?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, in Northern Ireland, in Ulster, but I would -- this is a court of law, not a seminar -- I would not wish to call the internment arrangements and prisons in Northern Ireland and Ulster in those terms. But, yes, I worked in Northern Ireland a great deal, but I don't think I want to call those "camps."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever -- that's why I phrased them "detention."

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the Mayes Prison is a detention centre of sorts, but I'm not going to call it a camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to. I was just curious to know how you reported those events, if at all --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: At length in Northern Ireland, yes. I mentioned earlier that I had won a prize called The Royal Television Society Award. That was for a film exposing Jerry Adams, his pretense that he had never been a member of the IRA, which we proved he had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vulliamy, you gave us some testimony earlier today and a little bit yesterday. Have we exhausted your recollection of all the events that you have for the period concerning Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that you've exhausted all of my recollections, but I'm mindful of the court's request that I be as relevant and brief as possible. I'd say we've covered the main ground, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And with respect to the conversations that you had with Dr. Kovacevic both in 1992 and in 1996, have you told us everything about those conversations?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: The conversation in 1996 was a long one, and I'm sure there was more, but I think -- I've faithfully reported the gist of both conversations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, during the time period that the '96 conversation took place, were you taping the conversation at all, videotaping?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I'm not a cameraman. The ITN pick and chose as they picked and chose in 1992; and in 1996, I was taking shorthand notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you have a videotape cassette player during the interview in 1996 between you and Mr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I don't carry a video camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it's your copious notes and your recollection that is assisting you relying here today about the conversation that you had with Dr. Kovacevic on or about the 1996 period; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely, and a colleague who was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And what was his name from New York --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: His name is Roger Cohen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you spell the last name just so we have it correctly?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: C-O-H-E-N.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I asked you about those copious notes and the records that you kept, handwritten copies, et cetera. Would those notes regarding the 1996 conversation you had with Dr. Kovacevic, were those also turned over to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At the same time you turned over all the other notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think maybe slightly after.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was it --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that. I don't remember which books I gave them when. I mean, I gave them what they asked for, and I'm not sure of the exact order, but I think I gave them the notes that they said they would need to have for the Tadic trial before those pertaining to the latter period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Was it before or after the Tadic trial that you turned over these books or notebooks? How would you like to refer to it so we make sure we're on the same line? Were they books or notebooks with your notes on them?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With respect to these notebooks, did you turn them over to the Prosecution after the Tadic trial or before the Tadic trial?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: After the Tadic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sorry. After my appearance in the Tadic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair, and I note that distinction.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So sometime in -- what? -- mid 1996 or ...

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, after that. This would have been last year, 1997, Kovacevic, after the Tadic trial, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to have to ask you this, it may seem boring to you --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Quite all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- trying to determine a little more about these notes, for obvious reasons perhaps. How long were these notes? How many pages were included in them, in this notebook?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the notes on the interview with Mr. Kovacevic, '96, about -- these are full A4 and slightly bigger notebooks, I mean, they're not pocket notebooks like this, and that -- I'd say five or six pages of shorthand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that I have a complete understanding. I'm holding a notebook. Would you classify this as a notebook?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, a hardcover notebook. Thicker than that and bigger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So when you say "bigger," it was longer and wider?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: A tiny bit longer, half an inch wider.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The five or six pages that you referenced, was that exclusively the notes that you kept with your meeting between you and Dr. Kovacevic?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. My notes of that conversation are about five or six -- I mean, maximum eight, minimum five A4, slightly larger than A4 pages of fairly close-knit notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Because I note the Prosecution asked you questions about Mr. Stakic, and I was curious to know if, within that notebook, you also had notes relating to your conversations with him and the other individuals --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it's in the same book. It was the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I recognise that it was the same day. How many handwritten pages do you have in these notes, including Dr. Kovacevic's notes that you took contemporaneous with the meeting as well as any notes you may have had from other meetings during that period?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: How many notes in the notebook altogether?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many pages? Sorry.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: How many pages of notes in the notebook altogether? Oh, a hundred, I should think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And were all 100 pages used to keep these contemporaneous notes and records of your discussions between certain individuals?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I like to keep big books which can often last me a month or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If this notebook is available, we should have it, shouldn't we, before the witness leaves? Are you going to finish this afternoon, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I agree with the former part. I think they should produce it, in the spirit of cooperation. I didn't get the last part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you going to finish this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Unfortunately, I am not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Keegan, have you got the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they were provided to us, and we have kept the notebooks for safekeeping, as Mr. Vulliamy, in fact, and part at his request, because he moved around, we retrieved them from Italy, in fact, where they were in storage, and he left them with us because he moved around so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where are they now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: They are upstairs locked away, Your Honour. We have never used them. And the typewritten portions referred to by the Defence were the draft articles for the interviews which were published in the newspaper, and they were provided to the Defence because they formed part of the supporting material of the original indictment in this case. So the typed part he referred to were, in fact, the draft stories he submitted to his own newspaper. Those form part of the supporting material. The Defence has been in possession of those since the time the accused was arrested and the materials were turned over. But as to the notebooks, we have never used them. They are his personal notes in shorthand, and they were only kept here so that, when he arrived, in preparation for testimony, he would have his notes available.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may briefly respond? Although we are interested in the notes that he took during his preparation period for the trial of Tadic and this one, I think Mr. Vulliamy testified that he kept contemporaneous notes during his interview, and I believe, based on my discussions with Mr. D'Amato and Mr. Vucicevic, those notes were never produced to us, those notes were never interpreted for us in any language, they were not given to our client so that he could review them, and I say this respectfully to Mr. Vulliamy, in order to verify the testimony being given and what's considered within his notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the notes would be the best evidence of what was said at the time since they were made contemporaneously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. As the Trial Chamber directs, we would provide them, but we were acting on the prior decisions of Trial Chambers of this Tribunal that those kind of things do not constitute statements of witnesses and that's why they were not disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clearly, they don't constitute statements, but they are contemporaneous notes, and I should have thought that from that point of view, if the witness -- if there is an application to cross-examine the witness on the notes, then that was something which we might well allow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, certainly, and as the application is now being made, we would certainly turn them over.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: We would like to apply to do that, and I think the best thing would be to recall the witness because it obviously can't be done between today and tomorrow, so would it be possible to have the Prosecution recall the witness at the point at which we are given some way of translating the shorthand and going over the notes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's very fair on the witness. If we can avoid recalling him, we should. It may be that overnight, the notes can be produced, the witness can have them --

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: They're in shorthand, I think. Right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt the witness can read shorthand, his shorthand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, they're in a mixture of a thing called T-line, an abbreviated ordinary longhand. I mean, if anyone reads T-line --

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: It's perhaps possible that the witness might be able to read them into a video cassette or something like that at his own leisure and pace overnight, and then we would have them in the morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, whatever is a convenient way of dealing with it, or to read them in court, but that may take rather a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: That would, we believe, Your Honour, perhaps be the most efficient and effective way for the Court to get the benefit as well. If the Defence has a particular question, based on the questions, for example, that I asked today, and the witness would have the notes, could read the full passage of that particular area, if that's what they're interested in. That seems to me to be the most effective way to deal with it so everyone gets the benefit of the full notes and we maintain some schedule of the trial. But we will produce the notes as soon as court is over today, Your Honour, if that's requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. D'AMATO
utterances.text: We will need some preparation time after we receive whatever form the notes are given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Keegan, you can show the Defence the notes and perhaps give them photocopies?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEEGAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be you'll have to ask the witness what the relevant pages are in the notes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'd be delighted to help to find them, yeah. I can find them very easily, very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. We'll try, if we can, to deal with the matter tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise for having to re-address this issue again, just so that I'm clear, it's not just his notes that were produced last year after the Tadic trial, I think -- and I'm just saying it because I was unclear during our caucus here -- it was the notes that he produced prior to the Tadic trial that he also tendered to the Prosecution -- I don't know how many pages those notes are. We only know, and my questioning was only limited to, the notes involving his '96 visit and conversations with Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But I'd like both just so that our request isn't mistaken to be a narrow one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The relevant notes, surely, are those which were taken contemporaneously. If other notes were made, for instance, if a witness makes a note at some stage in order to assist him to give evidence, which sometimes witnesses do but way after the event, then that's of no significance. What is of significance is any note which is made contemporaneously, and it's those notes which I had in mind, of the 1966 (sic) conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If any. I think it's the '96 conversation that notes were taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may inquire on this because it is a little confusing and I just want to clarify it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Clarify it with the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, again, not to belabour the point, the notes of 1996, the conversation that you had with individuals at the Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: The pages of shorthand of that conversation, I can find them easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- and of the other individuals that you had that you contemporaneously took and reduced to shorthand or writing, that was approximately 100 pages, that whole period of 1996 and the conversations that you had; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: A hundred pages is the whole notebook. I mean, that goes on to deal with a whole lot of other subjects and other places too. That's -- I mean, I don't change notebooks every time I change place or anything. I mean, the -- if I can help. The pages -- it's a thick book, and the pages with the interview with Dr. Kovacevic are six of some, I think it's 100-page or so book which is full of a lot of other stuff too, and -- but I can easily find the six pages which have Dr. Kovacevic, you know, written down on them. Likewise, the, I think, two or three pages that have Mr. Stakic and, yeah, I can tear them out or photocopy them or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, what we're going to order is this: That the contemporaneous notes of the 1996 interview are produced, not the book, because the book is the witness's property and nobody else's, and it seems to me the rest of it is irrelevant. But, Mr. Vulliamy, if you would please identify the six pages or whatever, the six pages plus --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can identify it already. It's clearly done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Once that is identified, it can be photocopied, and a photocopy will be given to the Defence. Tomorrow the book itself can be in court but, as I say, any examination of it is going to be limited to those relevant pages. So that I'm clear, having said that about the 1996 notes, have you any relevant contemporaneous notes of the 1992 conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the meeting in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've got some pretty scanty ones, yes. I'll have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We'll consider those in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vulliamy, we're done with the notes, and thank you. I think your one mic doesn't have a red circle around it, so perhaps if you'd depress the button -- it's okay?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Is that better?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, your duties as a journalist, can you generally describe them to us?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Chronologically?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, just generally, actually, not your professional experience as a journalist, but I'd like to know, not being a journalist myself, what your duties and obligations are when you do reports or when you report the news, if you will?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. You are assigned as your editors -- your editors assign you to work or as you recommend to your editors and then they agree in terms of place, theme, and your duties are to impart, when it was working for the television, it was research and set up and make films and to film whatever was going on, and for the print, to make the, now famous, as many -- as detailed and accurate notes as you can and to write it down and dispatch it, and then there are things called news stories, there are things called features, and there are interviews, profiles, book reviews, and they all require their own different styles, but the principles remain the same. If you're asking me about facts, the answer is you stick with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that you stick with the facts because, at the end of the day, the facts are one of the most important things during your process of being a journalist?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned these separate categories of the types of journalists there are, the feature journalists. There's also an investigative journalist; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. Most journalists do investigations at some point or other in their career, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And there's journalists who conduct documentary-type interviews; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: In television?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about in print?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: You don't -- well, documentary interviews in print? No, that's a term we wouldn't use.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What type of journalist were you, if you could categorise it for us, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was an all around reporter. I was responsible -- I was assigned to go to Italy, to be based there in 1990, and my brief -- my geographical brief was Italy and south-east Europe, and that included Yugoslavia. I think at the outset the idea was I would spend some time in Yugoslavia, I ended up spending a lot of time in Yugoslavia. I don't quite understand your question what kind of a reporter was I? I was a foreign correspondent.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you've answered that. I wanted to know what particular title that you had, and that would have been foreign correspondent; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned 1990. Prior to 1990, where were you stationed? You said 1990, if I can use the word "stationed" in Italy, but where were you prior to 1990?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was in London before then. I was the editor of the weekend section of The Guardian, until the end of '89.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How long were you the editor of the weekend section of The Guardian?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only a short time editing -- it wasn't the best thing for me at that time -- until the spring of 1989, I was a general reporter on the news desk at The Guardian, based in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Forgive me. I'm not as familiar with The Guardian as you are or perhaps I should be. What is the weekend section of The Guardian?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a magazine section that comes out in the weekend paper, Saturday edition.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Staying with this theme just for a few minutes because I'd like to -- is it fair to say that a reporter or a foreign correspondent such as yourself is required and under an obligation ethically, morally, and in every way possible, is under the obligation to report the news; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have an obligation at all to make the news?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, you don't have an obligation to make the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And isn't it fair that a journalist, a foreign correspondent, is not supposed to make the news but merely just report the news?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Now and then unavoidably you do make the news. This is particularly true of some of the more celebrated television reporters. You do make the news. Sometimes other radio stations or newspapers will want to interview you because of the sort of things that you do, but it's not an obligation, no, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The translating -- if I may just explain, we're waiting for the completion of the translation. Is it fair to say, sir, that the worst thing a foreign correspondent can do is distort the news?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Indeed. That would be very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there anything worse than that?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you could get killed in Bosnia, I suppose, but that would be an unfortunate thing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I couldn't agree with you more. And, quite frankly, I was -- my question was, and I apologise for not narrowing it, it was limited in your professional duties. There are other risks and things that are worse than that, but I'm saying professionally as a journalist, there is nothing worse than a foreign correspondent or a journalist of any kind to distort that which he has seen and that which he has heard; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: That would be a fairly serious matter, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned during your testimony, I believe yesterday, during the latter part of the hour, Serbs and then you started to describe that there were different types of Serbs and then I think you shared with us those concepts. Now, when you say "different kind of Serbs," historically, and having taken those classes, do you break them down into any time period or do you just collectively include all Serbs from 10 centuries ago or longer?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I've learned much more about Serbian people from my own personal experience than I have from books, and the point I was trying to make was that, too often, when people talk about "the Serbs" or "the Serbian view" of something or what "the Serbs" did, what they mean, and it's a forgivable shorthand, I think, they mean those Serbs who accepted this call-to-arms and to accept an ideology which I have described as nationalist. What I wanted to do with that remark was to make it clear that there are very large numbers of Serbs -- people of Serb origin, who find the nationalistic ideology associated with their people or which some of their leaders claim to adopt, or do adopt, as obnoxious, and there are very large numbers of Serbs who indeed fought against that in this war, so that's the point that I was trying to make, and I was wanting to, as it were, infuse my testimony with that rider so if I say , "the Serbs were shelling Bihac," what I don't mean is that all Serbs -- well, obviously some of them were shelling Bihac -- that all Serbs approved of the shelling of Bihac when it was quite obvious to me that very large numbers of them thought that was an appalling thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just going back, and I have one question on this. When you do an investigative report, isn't it fair that you would take as much information prior to completing your report, try to summarise it, have an understanding of a region or an area, distil that information, and then report that which you've actually seen and experienced?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you have to equip yourself, you know, as best you can. If you're sent to Belgrade at the end of July to report on camps on the 5th of August and you are to file -- I mean, there is such a thing as a deadline, and that story had to be filed, written on the 6th. So, yes, but the answer is: Yes, you equip yourself and you should be knowledgeable, absolutely. I mean, I could be sent to Lagos tomorrow. There's not much I can tell you about Lagos now, but obviously I would endeavour to inform myself about Lagos as much as I possibly could.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, I merely asked you a general question and I'm not sure if your reference was to the August 5th and August 6th deadline that involved some of the articles and the picture that was ultimately shown regarding the Prijedor area. Is that what you were referring to when you said August 5th and 6th? Were you under a deadline at that time?

utterances.speaker: EDWARD VULLIAMY (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I was giving you an example of how -- you know, you can't sit around -- if you've got a story, you can't sort of sit around reading library books for a few days before writing it because your editor will not allow you to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
